questions.q: What does a `.gitignore` file actually control?
options: It removes already-committed files from the repository's history
It tells Git which untracked files to leave out of git status and git add automatically
It encrypts all files in the repository
It prevents anyone from cloning the repository
questions.explain: .gitignore only affects untracked files — it tells Git to skip them when staging, but has no effect on files already being tracked.

questions.q: If a file is already tracked by Git, what's required before `.gitignore` will actually stop tracking it?
options: Nothing — adding it to .gitignore is always immediately sufficient
Deleting the entire repository and starting over
Running git rm --cached on the file first, to stop tracking it, then adding the pattern to .gitignore
Renaming the file
questions.explain: git rm --cached untracks the file without deleting it from disk; only after that does a matching .gitignore pattern actually keep it out of future commits.

questions.q: What does a leading `!` mean in a .gitignore pattern, like `!important.log`?
options: It deletes the file immediately
It negates a previous pattern, re-including that specific file even though a broader rule would otherwise ignore it
It makes the pattern case-insensitive
It has no special meaning in .gitignore
questions.explain: A leading ! is a negation, letting you carve out an exception — such as re-including one specific file inside a directory that's otherwise ignored.

questions.q: What is a global .gitignore (set via `core.excludesfile`) used for?
options: Patterns specific to one project's build output
Ignore patterns applied across every repository on your machine, typically for editor or OS-specific files
A file that lists every repository you own
It replaces the need for a project-level .gitignore entirely
questions.explain: A global ignore file handles machine-specific noise (like .vscode/ or .DS_Store) once, instead of repeating those patterns in every project's own .gitignore.

questions.q: Why isn't adding a secret to .gitignore enough if that secret was already committed once before?
options: Because .gitignore only prevents FUTURE commits of a file — it does nothing to remove the secret from the repository's existing history
Because .gitignore files are themselves publicly visible
Because Git automatically re-adds ignored files every hour
Because .gitignore requires a paid GitHub plan to work on secrets
questions.explain: A secret committed before being ignored remains recoverable from history in every clone and fork; the real fix is getting it ignored before the first commit and rotating the key if it already leaked.
